\chapter{The Core Verbs}
\label{ch:ta-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build a Tamil verb as stem plus tense plus person, swap the tense bead for past or future, tell a strong verb from a weak one by its doubled consonant, and say why \ta{தெரியும்} carries no person at all.}

Say \ta{எனக்குத்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{தெரியும்}, name the three slots that built irukkiṟēṉ, pōgiṟēṉ and pārkkiṟēṉ, and explain which slot \ta{தெரியும்} leaves empty and where its person went instead.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[iru]{\ta{இரு} (iru) — \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} and the machine inside every Tamil verb}

\label{lesson:TA-C32-iru}



\begin{quote}
Thirty-one chapters of words. Now the engine room. Tamil builds a verb the way you thread beads on a string, and this first verb carries the whole string.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{இரு}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{இரு}} — \emph{iru} — \textbf{to be, to exist, to stay}
\end{quote}

It is native Dravidian, from an old root meaning \textquotedblleft{}be, remain, stay put.\textquotedblright{} Kannada kept the very same word, \textbf{\ka{ಇರು}} (\emph{iru}), and Malayalam has \textbf{\ml{ഇരിക്കുക}} (\emph{irikkuka}); Telugu went its own way with \textbf{\te{ఉండు}} (\emph{uṇḍu}).

\emph{Iru} is about \textbf{existing} or \textbf{being somewhere}, not about linking two nouns. Tamil says \textquotedblleft{}I am at home\textquotedblright{} with \emph{iru}, and says \textquotedblleft{}I am a teacher\textquotedblright{} with no verb at all, just the two words side by side.

Its everyday first-person form is \textbf{\ta{இருக்கிறேன்}} (\emph{irukkiṟēṉ}), \textquotedblleft{}I am.\textquotedblright{} You have already heard it: the question \emph{eppaḍi irukkiṟīrgaḷ?} — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — is this verb wearing a different ending.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\ta{இ}} (the standing vowel \emph{i}) + \textbf{\ta{ரு}} (\emph{ru}) $\to$ \textbf{\ta{இரு}}. Both shapes turned up in \textbf{\ta{இரவு}} (\emph{iravu}, \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}).

In \emph{irukkiṟēṉ} the \textbf{\ta{க்க}} is held long — \emph{i-ruk-ki}, with a catch in the middle. That length is not decoration; a later lesson turns it into a rule.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem, then tense, then person}]
English changes a verb by putting words \textbf{around} it: \emph{I am, I was, I will be}. Tamil changes it by gluing pieces \textbf{onto the end} of it, always in the same order:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{இரு}} + \textbf{\ta{க்கிற்}} + \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{இருக்கிறேன்}}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{iru} (be) + \emph{-kkiṟ-} (happening now) + \emph{-ēṉ} (I) $\to$ \emph{irukkiṟēṉ}
\end{quote}

Left to right, the word says \textbf{be — present — I}. Three slots, filled in that order, welded into one word. Languages built this way are called \textbf{agglutinative}, from Latin \emph{glutinare}, \textquotedblleft{}to glue.\textquotedblright{}

Two payoffs arrive at once. The last piece already means \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} so \emph{nāṉ} is optional. And nothing here belongs to \emph{iru} alone: every verb in this chapter is the same three slots with a new first bead.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}iru\textquotedblright{} — be, exist, stay
  \item \textquotedblleft{}irukkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} — I am
  \item the three beads in order — \textquotedblleft{}iru … kkiṟ … ēṉ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three pieces of \emph{irukkiṟēṉ}, in order? (\textbf{Stem, tense, person} — \emph{iru}, \emph{-kkiṟ-}, \emph{-ēṉ}.) Which piece carries \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{The last one}, \emph{-ēṉ} — which is why \emph{nāṉ} can be dropped.) Which sister language kept the same verb? (\textbf{Kannada}, \emph{iru}.) Next: the same machine, with the tense bead swapped.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pō]{\ta{போ} (pō) — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and the bead that carries time}

\label{lesson:TA-C32-po}



\begin{quote}
You have the three slots — stem, tense, person. Keep the first and last beads still, and swap only the middle one. That is the whole of Tamil tense.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{போ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{போ}} — \emph{pō} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

Two letters, \textbf{\ta{ப}} (\emph{pa}) with the long-\emph{ō} sign, and a word so old it has barely moved. It is native Dravidian: Telugu \textbf{\te{పోవు}} (\emph{pōvu}) and Malayalam \textbf{\ml{പോകുക}} (\emph{pōkuka}) are the same verb.

Kannada's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}go\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\ka{ಹೋಗು}} (\emph{hōgu}) — and that \emph{h} is not a different root. It is the same softening of an old \emph{p} that turned Tamil \emph{pattu} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}) into Kannada \emph{hattu}. One sound-law, met once with numbers, now paying off with a verb.

You met the bare stem in the farewell chapter, where \emph{pō!} is already a whole command: \textquotedblleft{}go!\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: past, present, future — one bead each}]
Hold the stem \emph{pō-} and the person-ending \emph{-ēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) fixed, and let the middle piece do the work:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when} & \textbf{Tamil} & \textbf{the middle bead} \\
\midrule
now & \emph{pōgiṟēṉ} & \emph{-giṟ-} \\
already & \emph{pōṉēṉ} & \emph{-ṉ-} \\
not yet & \emph{pōvēṉ} & \emph{-v-} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textquotedblleft{}I go,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I went,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I will go\textquotedblright{} — one syllable of difference, sitting between two pieces that never moved. English needs a new word (\emph{will}) or a whole new shape (\emph{went}); Tamil needs one bead.

The tense bead voices to \emph{-giṟ-} after a vowel, which is why it sounds like \emph{pō-gi-ṟēṉ} here but \emph{iruk-ki-ṟēṉ} after the doubled \emph{k} of \emph{iru}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pō\textquotedblright{} — go
  \item the three times — \textquotedblleft{}pōgiṟēṉ … pōṉēṉ … pōvēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair that shares one sound-law — \textquotedblleft{}pattu … hattu\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}pō … hōgu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}irukkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}pōgiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} — one machine, two stems
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three beads changes for tense? (\textbf{The middle one}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I will go.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Pōvēṉ}.) Is Kannada's \emph{hōgu} a different root from \emph{pō}? (\textbf{No} — the same old \emph{p} softened to \emph{h}, exactly as in \emph{pattu} and \emph{hattu}.) Next: a verb whose stem refuses to sit still.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vā]{\ta{வா} (vā) — \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} and a stem with two shapes}

\label{lesson:TA-C32-vaa}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Pō} threads its beads on without a fuss. Its partner \emph{vā} does not — and the farewell you learned long ago has been hiding the reason.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வா}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{வா}} — \emph{vā} — \textbf{to come}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ta{வ}} (\emph{va}) with the long-\emph{ā} sign, and, like \emph{pō}, a whole command on its own: \emph{vā!}, \textquotedblleft{}come!\textquotedblright{} Native Dravidian, and the family keeps it: Malayalam \textbf{\ml{വരുക}} (\emph{varuka}), Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಬಾ}} (\emph{bā}), Telugu \textbf{\te{రా}} (\emph{rā}). Kannada's \emph{b} and Telugu's \emph{r} are two regular reshapings of the same old word, not three separate verbs.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word you say it by is not the word you build on}]
Thread the beads onto \emph{vā-} and you get nothing a Tamil speaker says. The suffixes attach to \textbf{\ta{வரு}-} (\emph{varu-}) instead:

\begin{quote}
\emph{varu-} + \emph{-giṟ-} + \emph{-ēṉ} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{வருகிறேன்}} (\emph{varugiṟēṉ}), \textquotedblleft{}I come.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Past: \textbf{\ta{வந்தேன்}} (\emph{vantēṉ}), \textquotedblleft{}I came.\textquotedblright{} Future: \textbf{\ta{வருவேன்}} (\emph{varuvēṉ}).

So a Tamil verb has a form you \textbf{call} it by — the bare command, the form a dictionary lists — and a form the beads actually \textbf{attach} to. For most verbs those are the same shape. For a handful of very common ones, of which \emph{vā} is the commonest, they are not, and the pair simply has to be learned together: \emph{vā}, \emph{varu-}.

You have said this word already. The farewell \textbf{\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்}} (\emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}) — \textquotedblleft{}I go and come back\textquotedblright{} — is \emph{pō} and \emph{varu-} standing side by side, and that \emph{varugiṟēṉ} is the very form above.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the command — \textquotedblleft{}vā!\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair that must be learned together — \textquotedblleft{}vā … varu-\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}varugiṟēṉ … vantēṉ … varuvēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the farewell you now understand — \textquotedblleft{}pōy varugiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What shape do the beads attach to for \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ta{வரு}-}, \emph{varu-}, not \emph{vā-}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I come.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Varugiṟēṉ}.) Which two verbs are standing in \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}? (\textbf{\ta{போ}} and \textbf{\ta{வா}} — go, and come back.) Are Kannada \emph{bā} and Telugu \emph{rā} different verbs? (\textbf{No} — the same Dravidian word, reshaped.) Next: a verb Tamil built for itself.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sāppiḍu]{\ta{சாப்பிடு} (sāppiḍu) — \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} a verb built out of two words}

\label{lesson:TA-C32-saappidu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Iru}, \emph{pō}, \emph{vā} — three single syllables inherited whole from the oldest layer of Dravidian. The everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}eat\textquotedblright{} is nothing of the kind. It was assembled.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சாப்பிடு}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{சாப்பிடு}} — \emph{sāppiḍu} — \textbf{to eat}
\end{quote}

Four beats: \emph{sāp-pi-ḍu}, with the \textbf{\ta{ப்ப}} held long, the same doubling you heard in \emph{irukkiṟēṉ}. Threaded up, it is \textbf{\ta{சாப்பிடுகிறேன்}} (\emph{sāppiḍugiṟēṉ}), \textquotedblleft{}I eat\textquotedblright{} — stem, then \emph{-giṟ-}, then \emph{-ēṉ}, with no surprises. Past: \textbf{\ta{சாப்பிட்டேன்}} (\emph{sāppiṭṭēṉ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
The word comes apart cleanly into two Tamil words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{சாப்பு}} (\emph{sāppu}) — food, a meal; the everyday \textbf{\ta{சாப்பாடு}} (\emph{sāppāḍu}, \textquotedblleft{}a meal\textquotedblright{}) is built from it.
  \item \textbf{\ta{இடு}} (\emph{iḍu}) — to put, to place.
\end{itemize}

Put food. That is all \emph{sāppiḍu} literally says. \textbf{\ta{இடு}} is what grammarians call a \textbf{light verb}: a plain, hard-working verb that lends its endings to a noun so the pair can act as one verb. Tamil builds a great many verbs this way, so \emph{iḍu} is worth knowing on its own. (Where \emph{sāppu} itself came from is not settled; treat the compound as transparent and the deeper root as open.)

Then the honest part. The inherited Dravidian word for eating is \textbf{*tiṉ-}, and it is thriving next door: Telugu \textbf{\te{తిను}} (\emph{tinu}), Kannada \textbf{\ka{ತಿನ್ನು}} (\emph{tinnu}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{തിന്നുക}} (\emph{tinnuka}). Tamil kept it too, as \textbf{\ta{தின்}} (\emph{tiṉ}) — now narrowed to chewing and snacking — and kept the old literary \textbf{\ta{உண்}} (\emph{uṇ}), Malayalam's \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ണുക}} (\emph{uṇṇuka}), besides. So Tamil did not lose the ancient eat-verbs. It built a new one and let them keep their smaller jobs.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sāppiḍu\textquotedblright{} — eat
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sāppiḍugiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} — I eat — then \textquotedblleft{}sāppiṭṭēṉ\textquotedblright{}, I ate
  \item the two halves — \textquotedblleft{}sāppu\textquotedblright{} (food) + \textquotedblleft{}iḍu\textquotedblright{} (put)
  \item the inherited root next door — \textquotedblleft{}tinu … tinnu … tinnuka\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words is \emph{sāppiḍu} made of? (\textbf{\ta{சாப்பு}}, food, and \textbf{\ta{இடு}}, to put.) What is a light verb doing there? (\textbf{Lending its endings} to a noun so the pair works as one verb.) Did Tamil lose the inherited eat-root? (\textbf{No} — \emph{tiṉ} narrowed to chewing, \emph{uṇ} stayed literary, and the cousins kept \emph{tinu}, \emph{tinnu}, \emph{tinnuka}.) Next: the verb that splits Tamil's verbs into two classes.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pār]{\ta{பார்} (pār) — \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} and Tamil's two kinds of verb}

\label{lesson:TA-C32-paar}



\begin{quote}
Four verbs in, one small thing has been inconsistent. \emph{Pōgiṟēṉ} has a single \emph{k}. \emph{Irukkiṟēṉ} has a doubled one. That is not sloppiness — it is a sorting rule, and this verb is where it gets a name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{பார்}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{பார்}} — \emph{pār} — \textbf{to see, to watch}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ta{ப}} with the long-\emph{ā} sign, then \textbf{\ta{ர்}} with a puḷḷi to strip its vowel: \emph{pār}, one syllable ending on the \emph{r}. From it comes the noun \textbf{\ta{பார்வை}} (\emph{pārvai}), \textquotedblleft{}sight, vision.\textquotedblright{}

Each Dravidian sister settled on a different everyday word for seeing — Kannada \textbf{\ka{ನೋಡು}} (\emph{nōḍu}), Telugu \textbf{\te{చూడు}} (\emph{cūḍu}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{കാണുക}} (\emph{kāṇuka}) — so \emph{pār} is Tamil's own choice, not the family's. But the family's shared root is here too: Tamil keeps \textbf{\ta{காண்}} (\emph{kāṇ}), \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} for formal and literary use, and that is the same word as Malayalam's \emph{kāṇuka} and Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ಕಾಣು}} (\emph{kāṇu}). Four sisters, one inherited root, four everyday preferences.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: strong verbs and weak verbs}]
Every Tamil verb belongs to one of two camps, and the tense bead tells you which:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{camp} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{past} \\
\midrule
weak — \emph{pō} & \emph{pōgiṟēṉ} & \emph{pōṉēṉ} \\
strong — \emph{pār} & \emph{pārkkiṟēṉ} & \emph{pārttēṉ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Weak} verbs take the tense bead lightly: a single \emph{k}, softened to \emph{g}. \textbf{Strong} verbs double it — \emph{-kkiṟ-}, held long — and take a doubled \emph{t} in the past. \emph{Iru} is strong, which is why \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{} was \emph{irukkiṟēṉ} and never \emph{irugiṟēṉ}. \emph{Sāppiḍu} is weak, like \emph{pō}.

There is no rule you can hear in the bare stem that tells you which camp a verb is in, so it is learned with the verb, the way a noun's gender is learned in other languages. Two camps, though — not twenty. Meet a verb once in its present form and it is settled forever.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pār\textquotedblright{} — see, watch
  \item the contrast, holding the long \emph{kk} — \textquotedblleft{}pōgiṟēṉ … pārkkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the past pair — \textquotedblleft{}pōṉēṉ … pārttēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item which camp each verb sits in — \textquotedblleft{}iru strong, pō weak, sāppiḍu weak, pār strong\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates a strong verb from a weak one? (\textbf{The doubled consonant} in the tense bead — \emph{pārkkiṟēṉ} against \emph{pōgiṟēṉ}.) Which camp is \emph{iru} in, and how do you know? (\textbf{Strong} — \emph{irukkiṟēṉ} holds the \emph{kk}.) Which Tamil verb for \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} is shared with Malayalam and Kannada? (\textbf{\ta{காண்}}, \emph{kāṇ} — kept for formal use beside everyday \emph{pār}.) Next: a verb with no person on the end at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[teri]{\ta{தெரி} (teri) — \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} the verb that drops the person}

\label{lesson:TA-C32-teri}



\begin{quote}
Five verbs, and every one ended on \emph{-ēṉ}, the bead that means \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} The last verb of the chapter refuses that bead — and Chapter 6 already gave you the sentence it makes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{தெரி}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{தெரி}} — \emph{teri} — \textbf{to know; to be apparent, to be visible}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ta{த}} (\emph{ta}) with the short-\emph{e} sign, then \textbf{\ta{ரி}} (\emph{ri}). Its base sense is not \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{} but \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{show up, be clear}\textquotedblright{} — a thing \emph{teri}-s to you the way a shape resolves out of fog. The everyday form is \textbf{\ta{தெரியும்}} (\emph{teriyum}): \textquotedblleft{}it is known,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}it is apparent.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil keeps a second know-verb, \textbf{\ta{அறி}} (\emph{aṟi}), for knowing by learning — the same word as Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಅರಿ}} (\emph{ari}) and Malayalam \textbf{\ml{അറിയുക}} (\emph{aṟiyuka}). \emph{Teri} has an exact cousin too: Telugu's \textbf{\te{తెలుసు}} (\emph{telusu}), from \textbf{\te{తెలియు}} (\emph{teliyu}).

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no person on the verb, so the person moves}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எனக்குத்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{தெரியும்}.} — \emph{enakkut tamiḻ teriyum} — \textquotedblleft{}I know Tamil.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Chapter 6 gave you that sentence whole; here is the verb inside it. \textbf{\ta{தெரியும்}} has no person bead, and stays the same shape no matter who knows:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{enakku teriyum} — it is known \textbf{to me}
  \item \emph{uṉakku teriyum} — it is known \textbf{to you}
  \item \emph{avaṉukku teriyum} — it is known \textbf{to him}
\end{itemize}

Only the little dative word in front changes. Tamil treats knowing as something that \textbf{happens to} you rather than something you \textbf{do}, so the knower is not the subject and cannot climb into the verb's last slot.

That is the chapter's closing symmetry. Five verbs carried the person in the ending, and \emph{nāṉ} could be dropped. Here the ending carries no person, so the dative word is the one thing you cannot drop. Telugu builds it identically: \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుసు}} (\emph{nāku telusu}), \textquotedblleft{}to me it is known.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}teri\textquotedblright{} — be apparent — then \textquotedblleft{}teriyum\textquotedblright{}, it is known
  \item \textquotedblleft{}enakkut tamiḻ teriyum\textquotedblright{} — I know Tamil
  \item the three knowers, one verb — \textquotedblleft{}enakku … uṉakku … avaṉukku teriyum\textquotedblright{}
  \item the five that carried the person — \textquotedblleft{}irukkiṟēṉ, pōgiṟēṉ, varugiṟēṉ, sāppiḍugiṟēṉ, pārkkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{teri} mean underneath \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{To be apparent, to show up}.) Which bead is missing from \emph{teriyum}? (\textbf{The person} — so the knower sits in the dative word instead.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I know Tamil.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Enakkut tamiḻ teriyum}.) Name the three slots one last time, with a strong verb in them. (\textbf{Stem, tense, person} — \emph{pār} + \emph{-kkiṟ-} + \emph{-ēṉ}.) Which sister builds the knowing-sentence the same way? (\textbf{Telugu}, \emph{nāku telusu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
